<reason>PRO built and defended the motion's core comparison (stock vs flow, compounding, human capital must be re-earned while capital need not) and kept converting CON's alternatives back into its own frame: if advantage is transmitted early through school fees, deposits and cushions, that is still transferred capital, which PRO's unified lifetime transfer base taxes and CON's does not. PRO also answered the two hardest pressures directly and concretely — the threshold/rate question (few million threshold, 50-60% marginal above it) and the "why more than loophole-closing" question (a soft effective rate still lets fortunes compound faster than they are taxed once a generation). CON fought well and made the sharpest structural move of the debate: narrowing the clash from "should inheritance be taxed" to "is the escalation justified," conceding taxation of previously untaxed gains and enforcement, so that PRO must show extra opportunity gains net of costs. CON's hits on instalments (deadline vs economic cost) and on the caricature of "waving fortunes through" landed. But CON's affirmative alternative was damaged by its own answer to PRO's Q1: it conceded private-company valuation defeats lifetime unrealised-gains taxation and fell back to taxing at death — i.e., PRO's chokepoint — while endorsing an annual 25% unrealised-gains levy that sits uneasily with its own objection about burdens on the living accumulator. CON's closing repaired the "ranking" mischaracterisation but not that tension, and its repeated "smaller estate is not more opportunity" refrain never engaged PRO's compounding arithmetic. PRO's two clipped over-limit turns are a real execution cost, and CON's discipline was better, but PRO gave the cleaner comparative reason to vote.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's Q1 ("which tax reaches a founder's unsold appreciating shares before death?") forced CON to either endorse an annual tax on unrealised gains or concede that transfer is the only visible chokepoint. CON did both — proposing a 25% annual levy while admitting private-company valuation forces collection at death — which PRO exploited in closing as CON taxing the living builder yearly while resisting the one unearned moment. CON's counter (appreciation is not capital stock; the levy applies regardless of inheritance) blunted the "concession of ranking" claim but left the internal tension about distortion on living accumulators unresolved.</best_rebuttal>
